metadata.title: What Does a Feature-Risk-Assessment Actually Tell You?
metadata.topic: FEATURE RISK ASSESSMENT · WORKING WITH CLAUDE
metadata.purpose: Answer whether asking Claude to run a feature-risk-assessment gets you a safe/not-safe verdict or a documented checklist. Lands the carry-out that the assessment tells you what to look at, not whether it's safe.

beats.narration_text: Someone wants Claude to approve a new feature before it ships — a clean yes or no. Wrong word: Claude doesn't approve features. It assesses them, against a fixed checklist. Will you assess this new feature?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'Claude, will you approve this new feature?', hesitates on 'approve', corrects to 'assess', lands the real question

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('approve' -> 'assess') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: It's tempting to think a risk assessment means eyeballing a feature and calling it safe or risky. Take one that looks harmless: users upload a photo ID to prove their age. A quick look says fine — it's optional, nobody's forced to do it. But the checklist asks a different question. Where does that photo go. How long is it kept. Who can actually see it. The quick look never asked.

shot.new_visual_element: A feature card gets stamped LOOKS FINE, then three unasked questions land underneath it one at a time

production_viz.label: A quick look, then the questions it skipped
production_viz.mechanic: A feature card reading 'PHOTO ID UPLOAD — AGE VERIFICATION' appears. A quick stamp 'LOOKS FINE' lands on it. Then, one at a time below the card, three questions fade in: 'WHERE DOES IT GO?' / 'HOW LONG IS IT KEPT?' / 'WHO CAN SEE IT?' — the card's border flashes accent as each lands, since the quick look never asked any of them.

beats.narration_text: Read the SKILL.md — one file, the instruction set, plain language. Then work through it: one step at a time, in order, no branching unless a step says otherwise. Watch the anchor: same feature, four boxes on the checklist — what's collected, where it's stored, how long it's kept, who can access it. Right now two of those boxes are blank. Nothing's been judged. Just documented, one box at a time.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR — the photo-ID card with four checklist boxes, two filled, two blank

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR — four boxes, two blank
production_viz.mechanic: A one-file SKILL.md chip appears, then a short arrow chain: READ -> STEP BY STEP -> RETURN. It fades. THE ANCHOR. The photo-ID card returns, now with four small boxes arranged around it, labelled WHAT / WHERE / HOW LONG / WHO. WHAT and WHERE fill in ('a photo ID', 'stored on a server'); HOW LONG and WHO stay empty dashes. THIS EXACT CARD AND BOXES RETURN, COMPLETED, AT B03.

beats.narration_text: Fill in the last two boxes and the picture completes: kept ninety days, visible to support staff. All four boxes filled — but filled in isn't the same as safe. Documenting where something goes doesn't clear it. And the reverse holds too: one flag raised here — no retention limit stated — doesn't mean the feature gets killed. It means someone now has what they need to make that call, instead of guessing.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — all four boxes filled, then splits into 'all filled is not safe' and 'one flag is not killed'

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — filled, then split
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 CARD RETURNS, identical placement, its two blank boxes filling in ('90 days', 'support staff'). All four boxes now read complete. It shrinks and moves up; then splits into two cards below: left reads 'all 4 boxes filled' with a struck-through 'SAFE' beneath it labelled 'documented is not judged safe'; right reads 'one flag raised' with a checkmark 'still a call to make' beneath it labelled 'flagged is not killed'.

beats.narration_text: A feature-risk-assessment doesn't tell you a feature is safe. It tells you what to look at before someone decides.

props.quote: A feature-risk-assessment doesn't tell you a feature is safe. It tells you what to look at before someone decides.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. Take one feature you're building or reviewing right now. Ask Claude to walk through it: what data it touches, where that data is stored, how long it's kept, and who can access it — before either of you says whether it's fine. Liam, in for Bear.
